desc:
Given a binary search tree and two integers low and high, remove every node whose value is outside the inclusive range [low, high] and return the resulting tree in level-order encoding.

Removal works like this: if a node is too small (value < low) it is replaced by its trimmed right subtree, because everything in its left subtree is even smaller; if it is too large (value > high) it is replaced by its trimmed left subtree. Nodes inside the range stay, keep their ancestor-descendant relationships, and their subtrees are trimmed in the same way. The result may be the empty tree [].

Do not rebuild or rebalance the tree; only cut away the out-of-range parts.

Tree encoding. A binary tree is written as an integer array in level order. The first entry is the root. After that, the left and right child of every existing node are written in turn, level by level, from left to right. A missing child is written as -1 (real node values are never negative, so -1 cannot be confused with a value). Missing nodes have no children listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped. The empty tree is [].

For example, [5,2,7,-1,3,6] is the tree whose root 5 has left child 2 and right child 7; node 2 has no left child and right child 3; node 7 has left child 6 and no right child.

Example 1

tree = [3,0,4,-1,2,-1,-1,1], low = 1, high = 3
Output: [3,2,-1,1]
Node 0 is too small and is replaced by its right subtree (2 with child 1); node 4 is too large and disappears.

Example 2

tree = [5,3,8,2,4], low = 6, high = 7
Output: []
constraints: 0 ≤ node value ≤ 100,000, all values distinct; the tree is a valid BST
hints: Look at the root first. If it is outside the range, which of its two subtrees can still contain valid values?
A root that is too small is replaced by the trimmed version of its right subtree; a root that is too large by the trimmed version of its left subtree. Repeat until the root is in range.

Once the root is in range, its left child only needs to be checked against low (everything on the left is already below the root, hence below high), and its right child only against high. Skip down while the child is out of range, then continue with the nodes that remain. Parse the array into child links, trim, and write the tree back level by level.
editorial: A node that is too small has an entirely too-small left subtree, so only its right subtree can contribute; symmetrically for a node that is too large. That gives the classic recursion trim(node): return trim(node.right) if too small, trim(node.left) if too large, otherwise attach trim(node.left) and trim(node.right) to the node and return it.

Each node is visited once, so the time is O(n) and the recursion uses O(h) stack space. The version in the reference solution is iterative: it finds the new root, then for every kept node skips out-of-range children (moving along the right spine for a too-small left child, along the left spine for a too-large right child). Finally the surviving tree is serialized level by level.
